rationale: A cold two-stroke engine run straight to cutting speed is more likely to bog or stall than one given a few seconds at idle first, and idle is also the safe speed to be at while a last look is taken around the zone before the line is actually spinning fast enough to cut.

title: Stage the blower at the work area
instruction: Carry the backpack blower from the rack to the marked staging spot before putting it on.
rationale: Staging the blower at the work area rather than shouldering it back at the rack means the first steps taken with a running engine on the back are steps that are actually needed, not an extra walk across the whole zone with a loaded backpack unit still warming up.

title: Bring the blower up to sweeping speed
instruction: Turn the speed dial up smoothly once the nozzle is aimed away from anyone nearby.
rationale: A blower brought straight to full speed with the nozzle still swinging around throws whatever is on the ground in whatever direction it happened to be pointed — turning the dial up only once the nozzle is already aimed at open ground is what keeps that first blast of air from becoming the first mistake of the sweep.

title: Sweep the path under the ground-watch's signal
instruction: Keep the ground-watch's signal steady, sweeping clippings clear of the path rather than across it.
rationale: The ground-watch is looking down the path in the direction the operator's own attention is on the nozzle and the debris, and a steady signal is what lets the operator trust that the path ahead is still clear instead of finding out otherwise from someone stepping into the discharge.

title: Check the hand-arm vibration reading
instruction: Read the vibration meter after the sweep and commit only inside the acceptable band.
rationale: Hand-arm vibration from a running power tool adds up over a shift in a way no single moment makes obvious, and a meter reading is what tells the crew whether this tool and this grip are actually inside what NIOSH's own guidance treats as manageable rather than just quiet to hold.

title: Scan ahead before sweeping the next stretch
instruction: Three things ahead change where this sweep can go — find them before the blower gets there.
rationale: A sweep planned only around what is on the ground and not around who or what is nearby is a sweep that eventually blasts someone's open car window, a pedestrian, or a loose pet — scanning ahead is what keeps the discharge aimed at clippings instead of at people or animals who never agreed to be in its path.

title: Keep the discharge off the storm drain
instruction: Confirm the storm drain is marked and sweep clippings away from it, not into it.
rationale: Clippings and debris blown into a storm drain do not stay there — they wash straight into whatever the drain feeds the next time it rains — so the sweep is planned to carry material away from the drain the whole time, not just when someone happens to be watching.

title: Close out the trimmer and blower log
instruction: Log the precheck, the zone posting and the vibration reading before racking the tools.
rationale: The tool log is what the next crew member and the next inspection both read — a shift run cleanly but never logged leaves nothing behind to prove the precheck, the posted zone and the vibration reading actually happened before the tools went back on the rack.

situation: A jogger has stepped past the near cone and is closing on the posted bystander zone while the trimmer idles.
instruction: Sound the warning whistle and wave them back before the trimmer comes up to cutting speed.
missed: The jogger kept closing while the trimmer stayed at idle. The zone was posted for exactly this moment, and a posted zone nobody enforces protects nobody.

situation: A gust has carried the blower's own dust cloud back toward the ground-watch, cutting their sightline to the path.
instruction: Angle the nozzle away from the ground-watch before the cloud reaches them.
missed: The dust cloud stayed on the ground-watch while the sweep continued. A blind spotter is the same as no spotter at all.

explanation: You aimed the blower's discharge toward a person instead of away from them. A backpack blower moves air fast enough to drive grit, gravel and debris hard enough to cut skin or reach an eye, and the operator choosing where that air goes is the only thing standing between a park path and someone getting hit with it.

You ran the trimmer with the cutting guard removed. The guard is what stands between the operator's legs and a nylon line spinning fast enough to strip bark off a sapling, and it also catches whatever the line kicks up before it becomes a projectile aimed at whoever is standing nearby.

You reached toward the trimmer head while the engine was still running. A spinning nylon line looks like nothing is there until it meets skin, and a hand reached in to clear a wrap or a jam finds that out immediately unless the engine is stopped first.

That wedge is holding the throttle trigger open with nobody's hand on it. The trigger is a dead-man control on purpose — the cutting head is meant to stop the instant the hand lets go — and defeating it turns a machine designed to stop itself into one that keeps spinning after it is dropped or set down.

title: Suit up before the site survey
instruction: Hard hat, eye protection and ear protection before walking the site.
rationale: Falling debris and sawdust from overhead pruning reach the ground long before the limb does, and the hard hat and eye protection are what the survey and the whole job depend on from the very first look up into the canopy.

title: Read the site hazard assessment
instruction: Check the job's own hazard assessment for the tree's lean, the line location and any flagged limbs before touching the pole saw.
rationale: The hazard assessment is where the crew's own survey of this specific tree — its lean, the line's location, any limb already flagged — gets written down before the work starts, so the plan is built on what was actually found rather than on what the crew remembers from the truck.

title: Walk the site before extending the pole saw
instruction: Three things about this tree change the plan — find them by looking up and around before the saw comes out.
rationale: A tree that looks routine from the truck is not the same thing as a tree someone has actually surveyed, and a line through the canopy or a dead hanging limb are exactly the kind of hazard a walk-around catches before the pole saw is anywhere near either one.

title: Barricade the drop zone
instruction: Cone both approaches and tape off the full drop zone before the first cut.
rationale: A drop zone that exists only in the crew's head protects nobody who was not in that conversation — coning the approaches and taping the zone is what turns the plan into something a passerby can actually see and stay out of.

title: Brief the ground spotter
instruction: Agree the stop signal and the drop-zone watch with the spotter before the pole saw extends.
rationale: The spotter is watching the drop zone and the line clearance from an angle the operator sighting the cut cannot hold at the same time, and that only works if both of them already agree on the stop signal before the saw is extended and it is needed for real.

title: Precheck the pole saw
instruction: Confirm the blade is sharp and guarded, and every pole section locks before extending.
rationale: A dull blade snags instead of cutting clean, and a pole section that is not fully locked can telescope shut under load — checking both before the saw ever extends is what keeps the tool doing what the operator expects instead of failing mid-cut.

title: Extend and lock the pole saw
instruction: Turn the locking collar to extend the pole to the working length and confirm it locks.
rationale: A pole extended without the collar fully locked can slip shorter mid-cut, dropping the head's reach right when the operator is committed to the swing — turning the collar until it locks is what makes the extended length something the operator can actually trust.

title: Check the clearance to the line
instruction: Read the rangefinder and commit only once the clearance is inside the utility's own safe band.
rationale: The rangefinder is what actually proves the distance from the pole saw's reach to the line, rather than trusting how far away the line looks from the ground — committing the reading only inside the utility's own minimum approach distance is what keeps this job on the safe side of a line nobody can afford to guess about.

title: Position the pole saw on the target limb
instruction: Carry the pole saw head to the marked cutting position on the limb.
rationale: Positioning the saw head deliberately on the marked cut, rather than swinging the pole around until it happens to catch the limb, is what keeps the first bite of the blade going exactly where the plan intended it to.

title: Brace and make the cut
instruction: Hold a braced stance and a steady grip for the full cut.
rationale: A pole saw held loosely kicks back toward the operator the instant the blade binds, and a braced stance held for the whole cut — not just the first bite — is what keeps that kickback from ever reaching the person holding the pole.

title: Cut only on the spotter's signal
instruction: Keep the spotter's signal steady, holding the cut only while the drop zone reads clear.
rationale: The spotter is watching the one thing the operator sighting the cut cannot hold at the same time — whether the drop zone is actually still clear — and a steady signal is what lets the operator trust that instead of assuming the zone that was clear a minute ago still is.

title: Confirm the limb has stopped moving
instruction: Wait and confirm the limb is fully still before anyone approaches it.
rationale: A limb that has just come down can still settle, roll or spring from tension in the branches underneath it — confirming it is fully still before anyone steps in is what keeps the moment right after the cut from being the moment someone gets hurt by it.

title: Buck and clear the limb
instruction: Buck the limb into sections, drag them clear of the drop zone, and stage the brush at the chip pile.
rationale: Bucking the limb into manageable sections before dragging anything is what keeps the clearing work from turning into wrestling one long, unpredictable branch across the whole site — staged at the chip pile, it is also ready for whatever the crew does with it next.

title: Close out the tree work log
instruction: Log the survey findings, the line clearance reading and the completed prune before leaving the site.
rationale: The tree work log is what the next crew and the next inspection both read — a prune done cleanly but never logged leaves nothing behind to prove the line clearance was actually checked and the drop zone actually held.

situation: A gust has shifted the limb's lean mid-cut, and it is no longer falling toward the planned drop zone.
instruction: Sound the retreat whistle and clear the area before the cut is finished.
missed: The cut continued while the lean kept shifting. A falling limb does not wait for the crew to notice the drop zone moved.

situation: A passerby has ducked under the barricade tape and is walking into the drop zone.
instruction: Sound the stop-work horn and halt the cut before the limb comes down.
missed: The cut continued while the passerby was still inside the tape. A drop zone with someone standing in it is not a controlled zone at all.

explanation: You made the cut before the spotter gave the clear signal. The spotter is watching the drop zone and the line clearance from an angle the operator cannot see while sighting the cut, and cutting ahead of their signal removes the one check that catches a bystander or a shifted lean before the limb is already falling.

You extended the pole saw inside the checked clearance to the overhead line. An aluminium or fibreglass pole saw does not have to touch a line to conduct — closing the gap the rangefinder already measured is closing the one distance this whole job plan depends on staying open.

You reached to pull down a limb that hung up instead of using the pole saw's own technique. A hung limb is holding tension nobody can see, and a hand or a rope pulled on it by feel is how that tension releases all at once, aimed at whoever is closest.

You are standing directly under the limb being cut. A limb coming down does not fall the way it is leaning right up until the cut lets go, and the one place nobody stands for a pruning cut is exactly where you are standing now.
